metadata.description: Contextual help topics for the Undercroft suite.

topics.title: Shared Workspace Layout
topics.summary: Each tool uses the same tri-pane layout with collapsible navigation, canvas, and utilities panes.
details: The left pane exposes navigation, palettes, and recent records. Use the sidebar toggle or the "Layout" button in the header to show or hide it.
The center canvas adjusts to the active tool: system schema trees, template layout boards, or interactive character sheets.
The right pane hosts inspectors, metadata, and contextual utilities such as JSON previews or collaboration panels.

topics.title: Theme & Accessibility Controls
topics.summary: Switch between light, dark, and system themes without reloading the page.
details: The theme buttons in the header remember your choice, so it stays set the next time you visit.
"System" follows your device or browser's own light/dark setting automatically. Every pane updates its colors immediately when you switch.
Tooltips and icons adjust to match, so contrast stays readable in either theme.

topics.title: Undo, Redo, & Keyboard Shortcuts
topics.summary: Undo/redo works the same way in every tool and mirrors standard editor shortcuts.
details: Each tool keeps its own undo history, separate from the others, so undoing in one tool never affects your work in another.
Use Ctrl+Z / Cmd+Z to undo and Ctrl+Shift+Z / Cmd+Shift+Z to redo. The toolbar's Undo/Redo buttons do the same thing.
Your undo history is remembered even if you reload the page or go offline, so you won't lose the ability to undo recent changes.

topics.title: System Field Palette
topics.summary: Drag fields from the palette onto the canvas to add them to the System you're building.
details: Each palette entry shows an icon and a short description of what that field type is for.
Drop a field onto the canvas to add it — the action is undoable, so you can safely experiment.
Number fields let you set a minimum, maximum, and step size once you select them in the inspector.

topics.title: System Field Inspector
topics.summary: Select any field to edit its title, id, validation rules, and computed values.
details: Changes you make here apply immediately and are saved as part of your draft.
Saving a System to the server requires Creator tier or higher — you can still build and preview one at any tier.
Computed fields use the same formula syntax everywhere in the suite — a formula that works on a System field works the same way on a Template or Character field.

topics.title: Active System Picker
topics.summary: Select an existing saved System from the server, create a New System, or Duplicate an existing System to create something new but similar.
details: Pick any System you own or that's been shared with you from the list to open it for editing.
Use "New System" to start from a blank slate, or "Duplicate" to clone an existing System (including one of the suite's built-in ones) under a new id as a starting point.
If a built-in System is briefly unavailable, you'll see a status message — everything else keeps working while it's sorted out.

topics.title: Template Component Library
topics.summary: Arrange reusable components—sections, inputs, tracks, notes—by dragging them from the component pane.
details: Every component in the library uses a consistent icon and name so they're easy to tell apart at a glance.
Dropping a component onto the canvas gives it sensible default styling and labels, which you can then customize in the properties panel.
Repeaters and Containers keep their own nested components together, with quick buttons to duplicate or remove them.
A rated/dot-style count (filled segments, e.g. Stress or Harm) is a Track, not a Toggle — Toggle is for a single named state, Track is for a count.
A single yes/no checkbox is an Input (checkbox) with one option — it stores the option label when checked, nothing when unchecked, rather than a plain true/false.

For content that only applies to one branch of a character (e.g. one set of abilities per sub-type), a Tabs Container with one tab per branch is usually simpler than trying to filter a single list by another field's value.
A computed field (a total, a modifier) is just a Text component with a formula binding (=sum(...), etc.) — see Bindings & Formulas Reference — not a separately stored value.

topics.title: Template Properties Panel
topics.summary: Configure binding targets, layout rules, and conditional visibility for each component.
details: Changes here apply to the canvas immediately, and each change can be undone.
Binding options are automatically populated from the active System, so you're always picking from fields that actually exist.
Advanced options let you adjust formatting, color accents, and responsive behavior without writing any custom CSS.

topics.title: Bindings & Formulas Reference
topics.summary: How @bindings and =formulas work across every Workbench field — syntax, available functions, and where each is (and isn't) supported.
details: Every content field in the Template editor has three modes, decided by how the value starts: plain text is shown as-is, `@some.path` reads a value from the character record, and `=expression` (an actual formula) computes one. Type directly into the same field to switch between them — there's no separate toggle.

`@path` is a dot-separated path into the character record (e.g. `@abilities.strength.score`, `@inventory.0.name`). It resolves the same way for every binding-capable field: Input, Track's Segments, Icon's glyph, Image's URL, Container's own heading, Text's Binding/Text field, and more.

Inside a Repeater's item template, `@path` resolves relative to that ONE repeated row instead of the top-level character record — `@name` there means "this item's own name," not a top-level `name` field. This applies to every component dropped into an item template, including a nested Repeater's own binding.

"Binding" and "Source" are two different concepts, not interchangeable words for the same thing: Binding/Text pulls a VALUE from the character record; Source pulls a CHOICES LIST from the System's own field definitions (used by Input's dropdown/radio/checkbox options and Toggle's states). A field labeled "Source" is not a place to type a value binding.

`=expression` formulas are JavaScript-like math/logic expressions, not a full scripting language — only these characters are allowed: letters, digits, and `+ - * / ( ) . , @ < > = ! ? & | % : ' " _ [ ]` plus whitespace. Object literals, template strings, and semicolons aren't supported; anything else in a formula fails outright with "Formula contains unsupported characters."

Both `if(condition, whenTrue, whenFalse)` and a real ternary (`condition ? whenTrue : whenFalse`) work — they're equivalent, use whichever reads better. Both nest freely: `=if(@dc, "DC"+@dc, if(@toHit, @toHit, "-"))` is valid. `if(...)` is an ordinary function call, not special syntax, so ALL of its arguments are evaluated every time, not just the branch that's returned — a nested `if()` in the unused branch still runs.
String literals need real quotes: `="Level " + @level` concatenates a literal string with a bound number. Unbalanced quotes anywhere in the expression will fail to parse.

A bound value used in a formula is coerced before your expression ever sees it: missing, `null`, and empty-string all become `0`; a numeric-looking value (including a numeric string like `"15"`) becomes a real number; anything else (a genuine non-empty string, an array, an object) passes through unchanged. This is what makes a plain `@dc` (with no comparison at all) the right "does this field have a value" check — it's already `0`/falsy when the field is null or absent.

`@path.someProperty` (including `.length`) only resolves when the bound value is ITSELF an array or plain object — a template's `.` traversal walks real object/array properties, not a primitive's own built-in ones. `@components.length` works because `components` is an array; `@dc.length` does NOT work because `dc` is a plain number-or-null field, and numbers have no such property to walk into — it resolves to nothing, then gets coerced to `0` the same as any other missing value, rather than causing an error. Use the plain truthy check above instead of `.length` for any number-or-null field.

String functions: `len(value)` — character count for a string, element count for an array. `upper(value)` / `lower(value)` — case conversion. `split(value, separator)` — returns an array (index it directly, e.g. `split(@name," ")` then use the result elsewhere in the same expression). `replace(value, search, replacement)` — replaces every occurrence of a literal search string, not a regex (there's no regex support — search text is matched exactly as written). All four take the value first, same argument order as `clamp`/`mod`/`pow`. Native `+` concatenation still works alongside these (`="DC " + @dc`).
Math and rounding functions: `abs(value)`, `ceil(value)`, `floor(value)`, `round(value)`, `sqrt(value)`, `pow(base, exponent)`, `mod(dividend, divisor)`, `clamp(value, min, max)`.
Multi-argument functions (any number of values): `min(...values)`, `max(...values)`, `avg(...values)`, `sum(...values)`, `and(...values)`, `or(...values)`. `not(value)` takes one.

`lookup(table, key)` looks up one entry from a named table and returns the WHOLE matched entry, not just one field — so `=lookup('abilities','str').color` reads the color property off whatever entry matched. `table` first tries to match a System field by name (using that field's own declared list of values); failing that, `table` is resolved as an ordinary dotted path into the same data every other binding reads. A key matches an entry by its sourceId, id, dotted key's last segment, name, shortName, or label — whichever the entry actually has.

`roller(notation, fallback)` rolls a dice expression (e.g. `roller("2d6+3", 0)`) and returns the total — only meaningful in Play/Edit, where it triggers the real dice roller and logs the roll. In the Template editor's own canvas preview it just returns `fallback` (or 0), since there's nothing to actually roll against yet.

Every binding/formula field shows a live feedback line right under the input as you type: a preview of what the current value resolves to against the template's sample data, or a red "Formula error: ..." message if it fails to parse or evaluate. This runs through the exact same evaluation as the real thing, `lookup()` included, so what you see there is what you'll get once the template's Data section is filled in for real.

That preview uses the template's own sample data, not a real character record — a formula referencing a field the current System doesn't declare, or an @path that's only meaningful inside a Repeater item, may correctly show no value in the preview even though it resolves fine once actually bound to a character.

Not every field supports every mode. A Repeater's own top-level binding only accepts `@path` — the value has to be a real array to repeat over, and a formula's result can't be one. Container's Label field, Icon's glyph, and Image's URL each support all three modes in one single field rather than a separate generic Binding/Formula control.

Colors (Text/Foreground/Background/Border) and the Visible/Collapsible/Locked toggles use this exact same `@binding`/`=formula` convention too — a color swatch's own Binding/Formula box and a boolean toggle's condition field both resolve exactly like every other field described here.

topics.title: Character Record Lifecycle
topics.summary: Load a Template, fill in your character's values, and keep working offline until you're ready to sync.
details: Selecting a Template builds out your character sheet from its components, keeping track of each one so your data lines up correctly as you edit.
Your work is saved as a draft in this browser as you go, even before you sign in or save to the server.
Saving pushes your draft to the server as a real record, keeping your ownership and any sharing permissions intact.

topics.title: Dice Roller & Formulas
topics.summary: Inline dice expressions evaluate with the shared roller and formula engine.
details: Type `/roll 2d6+3` in notes, or use the quick dice buttons, to roll and post the result to the game log.
Any dice-rolling formula on your character sheet uses the exact same roller as everywhere else in the suite, so results are always consistent.
Your roll history is kept for the session, so it's still there if you reload the page while playing.

topics.title: Relationships
topics.summary: Tie this character to any other record — an NPC, a Location, a Monster, another Character — with a label you type yourself: "Ally of," "Rival of," "Reputation with," anything.
details: Pick a target kind, choose the specific record, then type a relationship (a small suggestion list appears, but any text works).
Reputation with a faction or NPC works the same way — use "Reputation with" as the type, and the Value field to record where you stand (Friendly, Hostile, a number, whatever your table uses).
Relationships show up on BOTH ends automatically — link yourself as "Member of" an Organization's own NPC record, and that record's own list shows you back.
List shows every relationship as text; Graph (the icon next to the section title) shows the same data as a visual web, centered on this character.
Open jumps straight to the other record's own tool (Forge/Sanctum/Crucible/Workbench, whichever owns that kind).

topics.title: Sharing & Collaboration
topics.summary: Grant access via direct shares, reusable share links, or Campaign Groups.
details: The server enforces owner/admin checks before creating shares, and the record itself must already be saved — sharing an unsaved draft fails with a clear error rather than silently doing nothing.
Share links carry randomly generated tokens stored alongside the content id; access is logged for auditing.

A record can be shared with a specific user OR with an entire Campaign Group at once — sharing with a group grants every current member access transparently, and stays current as membership changes. See Campaign Groups and Sharing Content with a Campaign for the full picture.

topics.title: Group Members
topics.summary: Assign characters to a campaign group using the multi-select list.
details: Open a group row to see the Members picker. Click characters to add or remove them from the group.
Hold Ctrl (Windows/Linux) or Cmd (macOS) to select multiple characters at once.
Changes save automatically once you adjust the selection.

topics.title: Account Tiers & Access Gates
topics.summary: Feature availability is driven by user tier with graceful fallbacks for anonymous users.
details: Tiers, low to high: Free, Player, GM, Creator, Admin. Each saved kind (Location, NPC, Monster, System, ...) declares its own read/write tier — most generator output is wide open, authoring-heavy kinds need Creator or higher.
Tier metadata comes from the session token; anonymous users operate in read-only mode with local drafts only, saved to their own browser instead of the server.
Creating a Campaign Group requires GM tier or higher — running a game is what GM tier is for, distinct from Creator tier's focus on authoring reusable content (Systems, Templates) for others to use.

topics.title: Upgrading Your Tier
topics.summary: Self-service tier changes from the Upgrade tab — free for now, real billing lands later.
details: Pick any tier up to Creator from the Upgrade tab on your Account page, or the "Upgrade tier" link in your account menu — it applies immediately.
No payment platform is connected yet, so switching tiers (including downgrading) is currently free and can be repeated as often as you like.
Admin tier can never be self-selected here — it can only be granted by an existing administrator.

topics.title: Dashboard Widgets
topics.summary: A customizable landing page — build your own play space out of widgets.
details: Click "Edit layout" to add or remove widgets, and drag a widget's header to reorder it.
GMs get a Combat Tracker widget for running initiative, HP, and conditions; anyone in the group sees a read-only live view of the same encounter.
Your layout saves to this browser immediately, and syncs to your account too once you're signed in, so it follows you across devices.
Jump to any tool from the small home/switcher icons in the header — the Dashboard itself isn't in that list, since you're already on it.

topics.title: Second Screen Settings
topics.summary: Control the resolution, zoom, and placement of the mirror window used for a physical second monitor or TV.
details: Pick a common resolution, or choose Custom to enter any width/height your own second display needs.

Zoom scales everything the mirror window shows, for a high-resolution display that renders the same UI smaller than expected — change it any time, even while the window is already open, and it updates within a few seconds without needing to be closed and reopened. There's no scrollbar for the extra content zooming in produces; the table's own screen isn't something you scroll from the GM side.
In a browser that supports it (Chromium-based, once you grant permission), the mirror window opens on your second monitor automatically every time.
Everywhere else, the mirror window's position is remembered from wherever you last dragged it — drag it onto your second monitor once, and it reopens there from then on.
These settings live only in this browser, since a monitor arrangement is specific to this machine, not something that should follow your account to a different computer.

topics.title: Press Source → Template Flow
topics.summary: Press keeps the shared three-step flow: pick a source, map it to a template, then lock size and orientation.
details: Selections now live above the live preview in the center pane so source, template, size, and orientation stay visible while previewing.
Tooltips use the shared Workbench help system; click the (?) badges to open full docs without cluttering the canvas.
Overlays stay enabled by default so trim and safe areas stay visible in both preview and print stacks.

topics.title: Selections Panel
topics.summary: Collapse or expand the selections card above the preview to reclaim space on smaller screens.
details: The Source, URL/ID, Template, Size, and Orientation inputs share the center-pane card under a collapsible header.
Help badges next to the heading and Template label surface guidance without repeating copy in the layout.
After entering a source value, click Generate Print to pull live data into the preview and print stack.

topics.title: D&D Beyond URLs & IDs
topics.summary: Paste a D&D Beyond URL or ID; the value stays local while building your print job.
details: Accepts a character URL/ID, or a classes/backgrounds/species page URL.
Use an official or homebrew URL/ID; content stays in the browser for layout mapping.
You can paste a full URL or the numeric/slug ID from D&D Beyond; Workbench reads it locally for layout mapping.
Use share links when possible to avoid permissions issues while you preview cards or sheets.
Click Generate Print to run the Undercroft D&D Beyond parser and load the character into the selected template.

topics.title: 5e SRD Endpoints
topics.summary: Use SRD API slugs to prefill previews from the open 5e reference without auth.
details: Paste a slug such as `/api/spells/acid-arrow` or `/api/monsters/aboleth` to pull SRD data.
Requests stay client-side; nothing is sent to the server beyond the SRD fetch.
Pair SRD payloads with templates and sizes in the selections card to see print-ready previews.
Use Generate Print to refresh the preview with the latest SRD payload.

topics.title: Local JSON Uploads
topics.summary: Load a JSON file directly from your device; it remains local for preview and print.
details: Choose a `.json` file; the contents are read in the browser and not uploaded anywhere.
After selecting a template, map fields as needed so the preview reflects your layout.
Re-upload to refresh changes; use Generate Print to reload the preview and print stack with new data.

topics.title: Manual Entry Notes
topics.summary: Type quick copy for ad-hoc cards or tests without connecting to an external source.
details: Use this field for one-off notes, reminders, or draft text before wiring a source integration.
Content is stored in-page only; refresh clears it unless you save elsewhere.
Pair manual notes with any template, size, and orientation to see how they will print.

topics.title: Library Entries
topics.summary: Pick a kind and item saved to the shared Library, instead of typing a URL or endpoint.
details: Kind lists the entity kinds saved to the Library (class, subclass, background, species, variant, character, npc).
Item lists every saved entry of that kind, or "All" to load every entry at once as a list — one card per entry, the same way a 5e API list endpoint expands.
These files live under undercroft/common/data/ — most kinds are populated by saving from Loom's Entities pane, but npc entries come from saving a generated character in Forge instead.

topics.title: Mapping Description
topics.summary: A friendly name shown in Workbench's own player-facing "Import Character" picker, instead of this mapping's own filename/id.
details: Optional — an untitled mapping falls back to showing its raw id in that picker.
Only matters for mappings marked Data Type "Character" below (see Mapping Data Type) — that's the only picker this description shows up in.

topics.title: Mapping Data Type
topics.summary: Marks whether this mapping produces a full, standalone character — controls whether players can pick it in Workbench's own "Import Character" flow.
details: "Character" mappings (e.g. ddb-character) show up in Workbench's player-facing Import Character picker, letting any signed-in player import their own character directly, without needing Loom access.
"Other" is everything else — backgrounds, classes, species, subclasses, monsters, and any mapping meant for this Import tab's own multi-entity Save flow rather than a standalone character.
Purely a categorization tag — it doesn't affect how this mapping fetches or maps data, only which picker offers it.

topics.title: D&D Beyond ID or URL
topics.summary: A bare number or character sheet URL fetches a live character; a classes/backgrounds/species page URL fetches that content instead.
details: A plain number (or a character sheet URL) fetches the live character from D&D Beyond's character API.
A classes/backgrounds/species page URL (e.g. https://www.dndbeyond.com/classes/2190875-barbarian) scrapes that content page instead.
Character fetches are always previewable but never saved to the library — they're live/mutable and always re-fetched fresh.

topics.title: 5e API Endpoint or URL
topics.summary: An endpoint path or full URL; a list endpoint fetches every item in the list.
details: Paste an endpoint path (e.g. /api/2024/classes/barbarian) or a full URL.
A list endpoint (e.g. /api/2024/classes) recursively fetches every linked item's full detail as one array.

topics.title: D&D Beyond Monster ID or URL
topics.summary: A monster ID or monster-service URL fetches a live monster stat block (undocumented endpoint, separate from the character source above).
details: A plain number, or a URL like https://monster-service.dndbeyond.com/v1/Monster/16909, fetches that monster's stat block.

This is a different D&D Beyond endpoint from the Character source above. SRD monsters resolve with no login; a local server with server/ddb-session.local.json configured (same session-cookie mechanism as content-page fetches) may also resolve non-SRD monsters if your account has access.

topics.title: Fantasy Statblocks Markdown File
topics.summary: Upload a creature note exported from Obsidian's Fantasy Statblocks plugin — the data lives in its own fenced ```statblock YAML block.
details: Everything else in the file (frontmatter, the #monster tag, prose after the block) is ignored except a trailing "### Description"/"### References" section, which is carried through as this monster's own Notes.
Spellcasting is unstructured prose in this format — names/frequencies come through as-is, not parsed into real spell references.

topics.title: Markdown Item/Spell File
topics.summary: Upload an Obsidian vault note for a magic item or spell — structural markers (a #tag line, an italic type/rarity line, bold field labels) map to Effect fields; the rest is scanned for known Features the same way an SRD-imported Effect is.
details: Works with the markdown-item and markdown-spell mappings — pick whichever matches the file(s) you're importing.
A file's own name (not any text inside it) becomes the Effect's name, since none of these notes state their own name inline.

A file with no italic type/rarity line at all (a mundane/lore item with no real stat block) imports fine — it just carries no rarity/attunement/charges and whatever candidate Features its prose happens to match.

topics.title: Library Contents
topics.summary: Every saved item across every owner, with details and Share in the right-pane inspector.
details: Unlike the account page's Owned Content (which only ever shows your own saved items), this list covers the whole Library — every owner, every kind — since managing the whole Library is Loom's job.
Use the Type filter above the list to narrow it to one kind at a time.
Pick an item to see its created date, last accessed date, and owner in the right-pane inspector, along with a Share button.
Share opens the same access dialog used everywhere else in the suite — a public link, or granting a specific user or Campaign Group view/edit access.
This is separate from the Kind/Entity picker below it, which is for directly editing one entity's raw JSON.

topics.title: Library
topics.summary: Browse, edit, and assign every saved entity — Species, Classes, and any kind a creator defines, including Kind itself.
details: Pick a Type and an Item from the left-pane Library Contents list — that same selection drives both this JSON editor and the right-pane inspector (created/last accessed/owner/Share).
This is the only place saved entities can be re-opened and changed; the Entities panel above only ever shows the current mapping's fresh output.
A new Kind is just another entity: pick "Kind" as the Type on the left, New, and fill in id/label/plural/icon the same way you would for a Species.
Assigned Systems controls which System(s) can see this entity — an empty list means it isn't attached to any System yet.

topics.title: Assigned Template
topics.summary: Which Workbench Template a Character entity opens with — only entities of the Character kind that have one assigned show up in Workbench at all.
details: Narrowed to Templates built for one of this entity's Assigned Systems above — pick a System first if the list looks empty.

Characters are the one Library kind backed by the same ownership/sharing data Workbench uses, so this is also the only place a raw imported character becomes usable in Workbench: assign it a Template here.

The Template's own field bindings still need to match this entity's actual data shape to render correctly — assigning a Template doesn't transform the data, it just tells Workbench which layout to use.

topics.title: Features
topics.summary: The full structured editor for a Feature — id, name, description, mechanics, tags, and cross-references — not just Cost Budget/tags.
details: Select an existing Feature to edit every field: Description, Mechanics Type/Notes (see that field's own help topic), Categories, Behaviors/Recipe Slots/Roles/Creature Types, and Synergizes With/Conflicts With (references to other Features).
Useful for comparing near-duplicate Features (e.g. several "Dagger" entries) side by side — switch between them and see exactly what differs in their description/mechanics.
A brand-new Feature still starts on the Library tab (type an id there) — every other field is fully editable here immediately afterward.
Cost Budget is a rough points value (most Features run 1-6) — Crucible sums a monster's own Features' costs for display, weighted against its Combat Scaling level's own target budget.

Scope "Generic" means this Feature is set up generally enough to be used for any monster — the default, and correct for the vast majority of Features. "Unique" means it's not eligible for Crucible's native generation at all; don't assume a monster-specific-looking id means it should be Unique — check whether it's actually irreducible (2+ real mechanical differences from anything else) before marking it that way.

A note appears below Scope whenever a Feature has no Recipe Slots tagged yet — an untagged Feature is invisible to Crucible's own slot-fill regardless of Scope, so it won't show up in native generation until it's tagged. No note means it's currently eligible.

"Suggest Cost & Tags" asks an LLM for a starting guess at Behaviors/Recipe Slots/Roles/Creature Types/Cost Budget, grounded in the already-tagged starter Features and a real CR/budget calibration table — it never saves anything on its own; review the suggestion, then save if it looks right.

topics.title: Mechanics Type & Notes
topics.summary: What kind of ability this Feature is, and how it actually works — read by Crucible/Vault, not shown to a GM directly.
details: Type doesn't show up anywhere in Forge/Crucible/Sanctum/Vault's own generated output — it tells Crucible's and Vault's shared Feature editor which specialized controls to offer once this Feature is attached to a generated Monster or Effect there. Weapon Attack and Save Effect each get a dedicated attack-bonus/save-DC editor; Active gets a generic parameters grid; Passive, Passive or Triggered, Multiattack, Drawback, and Legendary Action Reference get no extra editing surface beyond this Feature's own fields.

Passive is the most common Type by far — a Feature that's always just true, with nothing to configure per-monster. Reach for Active only when a value genuinely varies per record (an ability score increase, a scaling number) and needs its own input.

Notes is free-form prose describing the mechanic in enough implementation detail to write or verify a stat block from — distinct from the plain-language Description field above it, which is what a GM reads. Not every Feature needs Notes filled in; many Passives are self-explanatory from their Description alone.

Picking the wrong Type won't corrupt anything, but it will make the wrong (or no) editing controls appear wherever this Feature gets used in Crucible or Vault — match it to what the Feature actually does, not to how important it feels.

topics.title: Macros
topics.summary: A dedicated tab for authoring Macros — the ordered list of actions a Macro runs when triggered, from the Dashboard's Macro board widget or a Journal note.
details: Macros are a real Library kind (creator-tier gated, shareable) — this tab is a purpose-built editor for that same data, the same relationship the Systems tab has to the System kind. The generic Library tab can still open a Macro as raw JSON like any other kind.

Each action row targets one widget type (WLED, Home Assistant, Soundboard, Handout, Combat, ...) — the fields shown change to match what that type actually needs (a device alias, an entity, a clip id, a contentRef, ...).
Actions run top to bottom — order matters (e.g. dim the lights, then play the sting).

A WLED action's device is a free-text alias, never a literal IP — the GM running the macro maps it to one of their own saved devices the first time it's triggered, so the same Macro works for anyone's own lighting rig. A Home Assistant action targets a live entity picked from a dropdown instead, with no alias step — the first time you try to use one, you'll be prompted to connect your own Home Assistant instance (a URL and an access token), remembered after that.

topics.title: Systems
topics.summary: A System is a set of Properties plus whichever Library entities are assigned to it — the same System concept Workbench's Template and Character pages already consume.
details: Systems are stored the same way Workbench already stores them (creator-tier gated, shareable) — Loom is a second editor for the exact same data, not a separate copy.
Workbench's own System Editor now points here for authoring; Template and Character keep working unchanged against whatever's saved.
Assigning entities to a System happens from the Library panel above (each entity's Assigned Systems list), not from here.

topics.title: JSON Preview
topics.summary: A live, read-only view of the whole System record as it will be saved.
details: Updates as you edit — every field you change above flows straight into it, so you can see exactly what will be saved before you click Save.
This is exactly what gets saved — the same data you'd see if you looked this System up again later.
Read-only — make your changes using the fields above; this panel only ever reflects them.

topics.title: System Properties
topics.summary: Each property is one field a Workbench Template can bind to.
details: The asterisk button toggles Required; the trash button removes the property entirely.
Default is applied when a new record is created. Minimum/Maximum only apply to Number properties.

This System's own physical dice (e.g. Daggerheart's Hope/Fear, Blades in the Dark's labeled d6) aren't a separate property type — they're an ordinary Array property with the reserved Key "dice": each value's Name is the die's id (what dice expressions reference by name, e.g. "2 hopeDie") and its Extra properties (JSON) box carries `sides` (a number, or "F" for a Fudge/Fate die) and, optionally, `faceMap` (remaps specific rolled values to a display label, e.g. a d6 showing "1-3"/"4-5"/"6" instead of the raw digit) and `color`. A System with no "dice" property rolls the standard 7 (d4/d6/d8/d10/d12/d20/d100).
Object properties can have Sub-fields (their own nested properties, e.g. an Abilities object containing Strength/Dexterity/etc.).

Array properties are either Enum — a fixed, System-defined list of values shared by every record (e.g. Rarity) — or Records — a repeating set of sub-fields whose shape (not values) is System-defined, so each record has its own actual items (e.g. an Inventory of Name/Quantity/Weight rows), with a Display field marking which sub-field represents each row.
Enum values' options row only enables the columns a value actually needs — see 'Array value options' for what each one does.

Every value also has an Extra properties (JSON) box as a catch-all for anything not covered by a column yet (e.g. a field-specific stat block) — it round-trips untouched even if this editor has no dedicated control for it.
Preview Data is sample data shown when previewing bindings in Workbench's Template editor — it isn't part of any real character's data.

topics.title: Group System
topics.summary: The System this campaign runs — its dice and vocabulary become the default for everyone playing in it.
details: Once set, this System's own dice (see 'System Dice') take priority over any individual character's own Assigned Systems for quick-dice buttons and rolls made in this campaign's context.
The Characters in group list below only shows characters assigned to this System once one is set — leave System blank to allow any character regardless of its own Assigned Systems.
Leaving this blank falls back to each character's own first Assigned System, and finally to the standard 7 dice (d4/d6/d8/d10/d12/d20/d100) for a character with no System at all.

topics.title: Group Setting
topics.summary: The Setting this campaign takes place in — used as the default for Setting-scoped System data, like the Dashboard's Calculator widget's Travel Means.
details: Optional — a campaign doesn't need a Setting the way it needs a System; leave this blank for a homebrew or generic campaign with no specific Setting.
A widget that reads Setting-scoped data (e.g. Travel Means, which can define means only available in one Setting) uses this as its own default unless a specific widget instance overrides it.

topics.title: Party Template
topics.summary: The Workbench Template this campaign's own Party Data view renders — lets a GM view/edit Group Properties directly, no character required.
details: Filtered to Templates built for this campaign's own System (set System above first); leave System blank to see every Template.

Author this Template's components bound only to @group.* paths (e.g. a Repeater on @group.inventory) — it's rendered with no character loaded, so any binding that isn't group-scoped just resolves empty.

Once set, this campaign appears under Campaigns in Workbench's own character picker — selecting it there shows this Template with Edit mode already available, and every change writes straight through, no Save button involved.

topics.title: Array value options
topics.summary: Which extra columns show on each of this property's values, and what each one actually does.
details: Binding — a generic @-path pointing this value at another field (e.g. @stats.hitPoints.current) — where this value's live data is read/written. Not specific to Role or Combat Bindings — any value on any array can carry one.

Description — flavor or rules text for this value, shown under its label wherever this Property's options are presented (a Select's dropdown, a Checkbox/Radio group's own option list). Without this on, a value's description still round-trips through Extra properties JSON instead — this just gives it a dedicated field.

Library-linked — each value can point at a real Library entity of a chosen kind (the Library kind field shown in the main Array contents row) instead of just being a display string. Turning this on reveals a Library-kind field and, per value, a select of that kind's saved entities — saving a matching Library entity later auto-links it by name, so linking by hand is only needed when a match is ambiguous.

Short name — a short label or abbreviation for this value (e.g. "STR" for Strength, "LG" for Lawful Good, "V"/"S"/"M" for spell components, "A"/"BA"/"R" for Activation's action-economy codes) shown anywhere full names don't fit. It's one shared property name used the same way across every Property that needs a short form — Alignments, Abilities, Activation, Spell Components, Sizes, and Speeds all use it — rather than each Property inventing its own name for the same idea.

Source ID — a stable numeric ID (typically a D&D Beyond identifier) this value can be looked up by. This is what lets a D&D Beyond character or monster import match a raw numeric code from D&D Beyond's own export (e.g. an alignment or condition ID) back to this value.

Source field — a different kind of pointer: the key of another array field on this same System whose values are this value's list of valid options (e.g. a Tags-role value naming a Conditions field), not where data lives but where the choices are defined.

Cost — a number each value spends from (or, if negative, refunds into) the active budget ceiling. Only meaningful on a Property that is NOT the one picked as Vault's Budget ceiling field (see that Vault topic): if this Property IS the ceiling field, Vault's own budget math ignores its Cost entirely and uses its Target budget instead. Turn this on for Properties like Activation or Item Form, where every value has a point cost.

Role — a small fixed vocabulary describing this value's structural behavior, useful anywhere it fits: Resource (a number with a max, optionally a temp buffer that absorbs damage first), Value (one standalone number), Tags (a multi-select status list), or Modifier (a number that feeds a die roll). Whichever array's values use Role is what the Combat Tracker widget and Workbench's character view treat as a System's live play-state (see 'Combat Bindings') — but nothing requires that to be its only use.

Target budget — a number each value sets as a target budget. It's only read as "the ceiling" from whichever one Property Vault's Budget ceiling field setting names; on every other Property, a Target budget value is just stored data some other consumer can use however it wants (e.g. Combat Scaling's per-CR entries carry Target budget for Crucible's own stat scaling, completely unrelated to Vault's economy). Cost and Target budget are not "pick whichever fits" — which one a given Property's values actually use is decided entirely by whether that Property is the current ceiling field.

A role's own extra metadata that's still just a single field's own quirk (Resource's max/temp path, Modifier's die) has no dedicated column — it's authored directly in that value's Extra properties JSON instead, the same as any other one-off property (see 'System Properties').

topics.title: Cost
topics.summary: How much this value spends from (or refunds into) the active budget ceiling.
details: A positive Cost spends from the budget; negative refunds into it (a drawback-style value, e.g. a Potion of Healing's negative cost representing single-use convenience).

Only meaningful when this Property is NOT the one Vault's Budget ceiling field setting points at — if it IS the ceiling field, this value's Cost is ignored entirely and its Target budget is used instead.
Turn this on for Properties like Activation or Item Form, where every value carries a point cost toward Vault's generation economy.

topics.title: Weight
topics.summary: How much a single unit of this value weighs — read by the Dashboard's Inventory Weight calculator.
details: Optional, and only meaningful for values the Inventory Weight calculator actually sums (e.g. currency denominations) — leave it unset on anything else.
A System with no Weight set on its currency simply contributes no currency weight; the calculator never invents a value.

topics.title: Target budget
topics.summary: The target budget this value sets — only counts as "the" generation ceiling when Vault's own setting points at this Property.
details: Read as the actual generation ceiling only from whichever one Property Vault's Budget ceiling field preference names (a Vault setting, not part of this System — see that Vault topic).

On every other Property, this is just stored data some other consumer can use however it wants — e.g. Combat Scaling's per-CR entries carry Target budget for Crucible's own stat scaling, completely unrelated to Vault's economy.
Cost and Target budget aren't "pick whichever fits" per value — which one actually gets used is decided entirely by whether this Property is the current ceiling field.

topics.title: Source ID
topics.summary: A stable numeric ID this value can be looked up by.
details: Typically a D&D Beyond identifier — lets a D&D Beyond character or monster import match a raw numeric code from D&D Beyond's own export (e.g. an alignment or condition ID) back to this value.
Only needed if you're importing data that identifies things by number instead of by name — most hand-authored values can leave this blank.

topics.title: Short name
topics.summary: A short label or abbreviation for this value, shown anywhere the full name doesn't fit.
details: One shared property name used the same way across every Property that needs a short form — STR for Strength, LG for Lawful Good, V/S/M for spell components, A/BA/R for Activation's action-economy codes, tiny/sm for Sizes, walking/burrowing for Speeds — rather than each Property inventing its own name for the same idea.

topics.title: Library-linked
topics.summary: Lets each value point at a real Library entity instead of just being a display string.
details: Turning this on reveals a Library kind field (e.g. "class") in the Array contents row above, plus a per-value select of that kind's saved entities.
Saving a matching Library entity later auto-links it into a still-unlinked value by name — linking by hand is only needed when a match is ambiguous.
This is what lets a System stay the roster (names, order, what's expected to exist) while showing exactly which entries already have real Library data behind them and which don't yet.

topics.title: Role
topics.summary: A small fixed vocabulary describing this value's structural behavior — useful for more than just combat.
details: Resource — a number with a max, optionally a temp buffer that absorbs damage first without raising the max — e.g. Hit Points.
Value — one standalone number with no max — e.g. Armor Class.
Tags — a multi-select status list, drawing its options from another array field named by Source field — e.g. Conditions.
Modifier — a number that feeds a die roll — e.g. an initiative bonus.
These are generic structural categories, not D&D concepts, and not tied to any one consumer — any array's values can use Role for whatever purpose calls for that shape.

Whichever array field's values happen to use Role is what the Combat Tracker widget and Workbench's character view treat as a System's live play-state (see 'Combat Bindings'), simply because that's the shape they're built to read — nothing about Role itself is combat-specific.

A role's own extra metadata that's still just a single field's own quirk (Resource's max/temp path, Modifier's die) isn't a dedicated column — author it directly in that value's Extra properties JSON instead (e.g. {"maxPath": "@stats.hitPoints.max", "tempPath": "@stats.hitPoints.temp"}).

topics.title: Binding
topics.summary: An @-path pointing this value at another field — where its live data is read and written.
details: Works the same way anywhere in the suite that uses @-path bindings — any value on any array can carry one, not just ones related to Role or Combat Bindings.

For whichever array the Combat Tracker and character sheet treat as a System's live play-state, this is the path they read and write for this value — e.g. @stats.hitPoints.current or @stats.armorClass.
Not to be confused with Source field, which points at where a value's list of valid *options* comes from, not where its own data lives — see that topic.

topics.title: Description
topics.summary: Flavor or rules text for this value, shown wherever this Property's own options are presented.
details: Shown under this value's own label in a Select's dropdown or a Checkbox/Radio group's own option list — e.g. a Blades in the Dark special ability's rules text, an armor type's own blurb, a Vice's own flavor line.

Turn this on for any Property whose values benefit from more than just a name — most enum-style Properties (Vices, Armor, special abilities, ...) do; a short vocabulary list (Alignments' short codes, tag names) usually doesn't need it.

Without this on, a value's description (if it has one) still round-trips through this row's Extra properties JSON instead — turning this on just gives it its own dedicated field rather than requiring hand-typed JSON.

topics.title: Source field
topics.summary: The key of another array field on this System whose values are this value's list of valid options.
details: E.g. a Conditions binding (Tags role) naming "conditions" so the Combat Tracker's tag picker offers exactly this System's own condition vocabulary, instead of a hardcoded list.

Generic, not specific to Role or Combat Bindings — it's a pointer to where the *choices* are defined, distinct from Binding (which points to where a value's own live data is read/written) and from Source ID (a numeric lookup id, not a field reference).
Most commonly meaningful on a Tags-role value, but nothing about it is tags-specific — any value that needs its options sourced from another field can use it.

topics.title: Combat Bindings
topics.summary: Which ordinary Array property holds this System's live combat state, and how each of its values behaves.
details: Combat Bindings isn't its own property type — it's simply whichever Array property has values that use Role (Resource, Value, Tags, or Modifier). The Combat Tracker and character sheet both look for that shape and read/write it during play.

Each value names a Role plus a Binding (the path into a character it reads and writes), so the shape is entirely up to you: add as many or as few bound values as your game actually needs, with whatever names make sense — Hit Points, Sanity, Armor Class, Conditions, Initiative, and so on. A Tags-role value also names a Source field, the other array field supplying its valid options.
A role that needs more than one path or other extra detail (like a Resource's separate max value) doesn't get its own column — add it to that value's Extra properties instead.
If a System has no array using Role at all, the Combat Tracker and character sheet simply won't show live combat state for it — nothing breaks.

topics.title: Setting
topics.summary: Choose which Setting this Location belongs to — its Name and Description are edited under Setting Properties in the right pane.
details: A Setting belongs to one System (e.g. Forgotten Realms under D&D 5E); every Location belongs to one Setting (e.g. Sword Coast under Forgotten Realms).
Leave this blank to start a new Setting (New in Setting Properties), or pick an existing one here to edit it or add Locations to it.

topics.title: Location Properties
topics.summary: Optional per-Location settings Forge uses to generate NPCs here — not every place needs one.
details: Species Weights, Mixing Coefficient, and Setting-Specific Archetypes drive Forge's weighted species roll and name blending for this Location specifically.

Species Weights here take priority over the Setting's own default Species Weights (Setting Properties, right pane) — leave this Location's own list empty to fall back to the Setting's general population instead of defining one from scratch.

Generic Name Fallback: names to draw from when a rolled species is "Other" or otherwise can't be resolved to a real Species entity. Each entry is a name and an optional weight (defaults to 1 if left blank) — higher weight means more likely to be picked.
Leave this whole section empty for a Location that will never be used to generate NPCs (a Room, a Structure with no population).

topics.title: Species Weights
topics.summary: Optional. The Setting's own general population — the default Forge falls back to for any Location here with no Species Weights of its own.
details: Same shape as a Location's own Species Weights (Location Properties, center pane): pick a Species and a relative weight for each entry Forge should be able to roll.
A Location's own Species Weights always take priority when it has any — this is only ever used when that Location's list is empty (or no Location is selected at all).
Leave this empty if every Location in this Setting will always define its own population explicitly.

topics.title: Calendar
topics.summary: Optional. In-fiction calendar vocabulary for this Setting — days per week, weekday names, months, and moon cycles.
details: Months is the only field a real calendar needs: an ordered list of names with a day count each (e.g. Eberron's 13 months of 28 days), handling uneven real-world-style month lengths just as well.
Weekday names and moon cycles are optional extras — leave them empty if this Setting doesn't need a week or moon-phase tracking.
Leave the whole section empty for a Setting that will never use a Dashboard Calendar widget — a Calendar widget can only be added against a Setting that actually has one defined here.

topics.title: Template & Size Pairing
topics.summary: Template choices drive supported sizes and orientations, which auto-refresh when the template changes.
details: Format and orientation dropdowns sit on their own rows so each choice stays visible while you scroll other inputs.
Selections stay in the center pane above the preview, keeping template and size choices in view.
Changing templates resets the size and orientation dropdowns before rebuilding the preview and print stack.

topics.title: Selecting Print Size
topics.summary: Size options come from the chosen template; pick the paper size that matches your stock.
details: Templates surface only supported sizes; switching templates refreshes this list automatically.
Use the selections card to confirm the active size before printing.
Card templates factor in gutters and margins when calculating the printable grid for each size.

topics.title: Choosing Orientation
topics.summary: Orientation defaults to the template recommendation but can be changed per format.
details: Orientation options depend on the selected size; some formats may offer only portrait or landscape.
Switching orientation rebuilds the preview and print stack to fit the new layout.
Trim and safe overlays adjust automatically so you can validate margins before printing.

topics.title: Press Palette
topics.summary: Drag components from the left pane into the preview canvas or layout outline to build each side.
details: Drop palette items directly onto the live preview; the layout outline updates in sync and selects the new component.
Double-click a palette row to append it to the end of the current side when you do not want to drag.
Palette clones share a Sortable group with the layout so you can reorder items either in the outline or on the page.

topics.title: Global Sample Data
topics.summary: Edit the shared JSON used for previews when no source data is loaded, or review loaded data when available.
details: Changes are saved automatically to local storage.
Valid JSON updates the preview immediately; invalid JSON is highlighted until corrected.
When source data is loaded, this panel switches to display the loaded payload instead of the sample JSON.

topics.title: Page Bindings
topics.summary: Control which data scope each side uses and which collections repeat across grids.
details: Data bindings set the root context for a side so all bindings resolve from a sub-object instead of the full payload.
Repeat bindings are used for card/chip grids to iterate over a list such as @features or @attacks.
Leave data blank to keep the full source payload in scope for the current side.

topics.title: Layout Canvas & Outline
topics.summary: Use the right-pane outline or the on-page drag handles to change the order of components for the current side.
details: Drop palette items into the preview page to add them where you want; the outline mirrors the order automatically.
Reorder items in the layout list or directly on the canvas—both paths update the live preview and print stack.
Each side keeps its own layout; switch sides with the toggle above the preview to edit front and back separately.

topics.title: Component Inspector
topics.summary: Select any component on the page or outline to edit its text, font size, color, visibility, and heading level.
details: When a component is selected, the inspector enables inputs for text, sizing, color, visibility, and heading level.
List components treat each line in the text area as a separate list item so you can build bullet lists quickly.
Toggles and sliders update the preview immediately, keeping the print stack synchronized with your changes.

topics.title: Alignment & Print Prep
topics.summary: Follow the four-step alignment checklist before printing cards, notecards, or sheets.
details: Overlays stay visible in preview and print; measure the 0.25in margins and confirm cut lines align across sides.
Verify that dashed safe areas stay inside the inset guides and run a test sheet before bulk jobs.
Use system print dialogs with 100% scaling and flip on the long edge for duplex output.

topics.title: Generating an NPC
topics.summary: Pick a Location, then Generate NPC to roll a full Identity + 4D set for it.
details: The Location determines Species weights and the two setting-specific Archetype entries (rolls 22-23) — everything else (Alignment, Gender, Attitude, and the 4D tables) is the same everywhere.
Generate NPC rolls every attribute at once. Once generated, each Identity/4D value in the main pane has its own reroll button if you just want to redo one thing.
Species, Archetype, Alignment, and Gender can each be fixed to a specific value instead of rolled — see the help on those selects below.
The character note is optional and separate — generate one afterward from the main pane if you want it.

topics.title: Fixing Specific Attributes
topics.summary: Pick a Species, Archetype, Alignment, or Gender to use that exact value instead of rolling it — leave any of them on "Random" to roll as usual.
details: Each select defaults to "Random". Choosing a value there locks that one attribute for the next Generate NPC click — everything you didn't pick still rolls normally.
Species and Archetype options come from the selected Location, since both are location-configured; Alignment and Gender are the same everywhere and don't change with Location.
These only affect the initial Generate NPC roll — the per-attribute reroll buttons on an already-generated NPC always roll fresh, ignoring whatever's picked here.

topics.title: Mixing Coefficient
topics.summary: One 0-1 dial that controls how much this Location's species blend together when generating a Name — 0 is culturally isolated, 1 is fully cosmopolitan.
details: At 0, names never blend — every NPC gets a plain name from its own species. As the coefficient rises, blended names (a name shaped by two species at once) start happening, more often and more deeply the higher it goes.

The same number also decides who a name blends with: at low values the blend partner is always this Location's single most common species; at high values it's a weighted-random pick from the whole population, so blending gets more varied as well as more frequent.

It also decides how deep a blend goes: low values favor a light surface borrow (one species' name with a short flourish from another); high values favor a deeper blend where the name itself is genuinely shaped by both species.
At 1, blending always happens, the partner is always randomly drawn, and the deepest blend mode is always used — nothing here is ever a hard on/off switch, just more or less likely.

topics.title: Species Name Profiles
topics.summary: One name per line, per pool — a Species' own list of example names Forge draws from, generated fresh (Blended mode) or picked as-is (Synonyms mode) depending on Name Mode.
details: In Blended mode, First Names (and Last Names, if this species has them) are example pools Forge studies the patterns of, producing new names that sound like they belong without ever handing back an exact line verbatim — more and more varied examples produce more varied results, so a pool of 20-30 real names per list works well.
In Synonyms mode, the pool is drawn from directly instead — see the Name Mode help below for when to use it and why.
Last Name Form only controls the label shown (Family, Clan, Patronymic) and whether a last name is generated at all — set it to None for species that only ever use a single name.
A profile saved here is reusable across every Location, not just the one you were editing from — Species Weights rows in any Location can select it.

topics.title: Name Mode: Blended vs. Synonyms
topics.summary: Blended generates novel invented names by statistically recombining the pool's phonetic patterns; Synonyms just draws a name from the pool as-is, unmodified.
details: Use Blended for species whose names are an invented phonetic language (Elf, Dwarf, Tiefling, most humanoid species) — the shared sub-word patterns across the pool (endings, syllable clusters) are what make recombination sound plausible.

Use Synonyms for species whose names are recognizable whole words in a shared thematic register instead (Changeling's Ashen/Doubt/Mirage, Warforged's Rivet/Piston/Bastion, Shifter's Wren/Briar/Talon) — recombining letters across words like that just produces garbage, since there's no shared phonetic pattern to learn. Synonyms mode instead treats the pool as a curated, closed vocabulary and draws directly from it.

Synonyms-mode species never take part in cultural mixing, in either direction — a curated whole word can't be sensibly blended with another species' name, so a Synonyms-mode species is skipped both as a blend primary and as a possible blend partner, regardless of the Location's Mixing Coefficient.
This is a per-species setting, not per-Location — a species is either invented-phonetic or curated-vocabulary everywhere it's used.

topics.title: Identity Attributes
topics.summary: System- and setting-specific categorical attributes shaped by the selected Location — who this NPC is in the world.
details: Species, Archetype, Alignment, Gender, Age, Relationship, and Attitude all describe concrete facts about this specific NPC.

Species and Archetype are location-configured, coming straight from the selected Location's own tables; Alignment, Gender, Age, Relationship, and Attitude are the same everywhere and never change with Location.
This is what changes most between locations and settings — the 4D attributes below never do.

topics.title: 4D Attributes
topics.summary: System-agnostic personality and situation prompts — improv material, not prescriptions, and identical no matter the Location or game system.
details: Description, Demeanor, Drive, and Direction are single-word improv prompts designed to stack: rolling the same table twice can produce interesting tension rather than a contradiction.
Unlike Identity, these never vary by Location or game system — they're meant to work for any NPC in any setting.
Treat them as a starting point for roleplay, not a fixed personality description.

topics.title: Stats
topics.summary: Ability scores, AC, and HP come straight from the D&D5e Monster Manual NPC stat block matching this NPC's Archetype — nothing here is rolled.
details: These aren't independent rolls: they're looked up by Archetype, so they update automatically whenever Archetype is generated or rerolled.
Setting-specific archetypes (rolls 22-23) and Wildcard (roll 24) have no fixed identity, so no stat block exists for them — you'll see a note instead of numbers.
Only D&D5e is supported right now, matching the rest of Forge's Archetype table.

topics.title: Notes (optional)
topics.summary: Optional. Type your own note directly, or use Generate Note to have Claude write one from the rolled attributes — either way you can freely edit it afterward.
details: An NPC is complete without a note — every rolled value already stands on its own as the character record.
Generate Note sends the rolled Identity (minus Name) and 4D values to Claude and fills this box with its response in a fixed format: Name (Alignment Gender Species Archetype). [2-3 sentences].
Whatever's in the box when you Save is what gets saved — write your own from scratch, or generate one and edit it.

topics.title: Relationships
topics.summary: Tie this NPC to any other record — another NPC, a Location, a Monster, a Character — with a label you type yourself: "Member of," "Leads," "Enemy of," anything.
details: Pick a target kind, choose the specific record, then type a relationship (a small suggestion list appears, but any text works).

Relationships show up on BOTH ends automatically — add "Member of" from three different NPCs pointing at the same one, and that one's own list shows all three members right back, with no extra setup. That's also how a Faction works here: there's no separate Organization type to pick, an NPC just becomes one the moment other records relate to it that way.
List shows every relationship as text; Graph (the icon next to the section title) shows the same data as a visual web, centered on this NPC.
Open jumps straight to the other record's own tool (Forge/Sanctum/Crucible/Workbench, whichever owns that kind).

topics.title: Species Weights
topics.summary: Each row picks a saved Species Name Profile and its relative weight for this location — this is what Forge draws from to roll a new NPC's Species and Name.
details: Each row's select lists every species profile saved via Manage Species — create one there first if the species you want isn't listed yet, then it'll show up here.
Weights are relative to each other, not percentages — they don't need to sum to 100 or any other fixed total, only to reflect roughly how common each species is here.
This population (combined with the Mixing Coefficient below) is what makes two locations both sound and feel different even though every other Identity/4D table is shared.

topics.title: Setting-Specific Archetypes
topics.summary: Fills the D&D5e archetype table's two location-overridable rolls (22 and 23) with entries specific to this location.
details: The archetype table is 2d12: rolls 2-21 and 24 (Wildcard) are fixed and never change regardless of location.
Rolls 22 and 23 are reserved for setting-specific archetypes — enter whatever fits this location (a local guard title, a regional faction agent, etc.).
Leaving either blank falls back to a generic "Setting Specific" placeholder when that roll comes up.

topics.title: Component Properties
topics.summary: Select any box in Identity to inspect it here — Species and Location open their full editors, everything else shows the JSON data driving that roll.
details: Species and Location are reusable configuration (a Species Name Profile, a saved Location), so selecting either opens the same full editor as Manage Species / Manage Location.
Every other Identity box (Name, Archetype, Alignment, Gender, Age, Relationship, Attitude) shows the complete table or profile data behind that roll, alongside this NPC's current rolled value.
Nothing shows here until something in Identity is selected.

topics.title: Campaign Groups
topics.summary: A Campaign Group is how a GM organizes a table: an owner, a roster of member characters, a live game log, and a public share link.
details: Create one from Loom's Groups tab — requires GM tier or higher.
Add players' characters to the roster from the same tab — this is what determines who can see the group's game log while signed in.
Every group gets a public share link (also from the Groups tab) so players without an account can watch the game log and claim an unclaimed character.

topics.title: Active Campaign Selector
topics.summary: The signed-in menu in every tool's header picks which of your own groups is "active" right now — the same selection follows you across every tool.
details: Only your OWN groups (ones you created) show up here — it lists exactly what Loom's Groups tab lists for you.

Picking a group here is what "Share with [active campaign]" one-click buttons target, and which campaign the Dashboard's own widgets (Handout, Combat Tracker, ...) read from — no separate per-tool setup needed.
The selection is stored per-browser (not on the server against your account), so switching computers means picking it again.

topics.title: Sharing Content with a Campaign
topics.summary: Any saved record — a Location, NPC, Monster, Effect, Map, System, Template — can be shared with a specific person or an entire campaign group at once.
details: Sharing with a group grants every current member access transparently — one action instead of sharing with each player individually, and it stays current as membership changes.

Share dialogs across the suite (Loom's Library inspector, the account page's Owned Content tab, and per-tool inspectors) offer a one-click "Share with [active campaign]" button alongside the full user/group picker once you have an active campaign selected.
Shares carry "view" or "edit" permission — view is the right choice for almost everything shared with players.

topics.title: Handouts / Now Showing
topics.summary: Put one card up in front of the table live — add a Handout widget to your own Dashboard and click its visibility icon, no exporting or switching to Press yourself.
details: Add a Handout from the Dashboard's Edit-layout toolbar: pick the record (an NPC, Location, Monster, or Effect) and, optionally, a Press print template to render it with — with no template picked, the table sees a plain name/description card instead.
Click the eye icon on the Handout's header to show it to your active campaign, and again to stop — the icon reflects whatever's actually visible right now, even after a reload.
The record must already be SAVED first — showing something that only exists as an unsaved draft fails immediately with a clear error, rather than silently showing nothing to the table.
Maps work the same way from a Map widget instead, or from Orrery's own signed-in menu — a map is always a plain link back into Orrery, never a card.
Whoever's watching sees it in Workbench's "Now Showing" panel, next to the Game Log — including anonymous players on the group's public share link.

topics.title: Game Log
topics.summary: A live, lightweight feed of dice rolls, messages, and spotlighted cards for a campaign group — visible in Workbench, polling every 30 seconds.
details: Shows automatically once Workbench has a group to follow: either a loaded character's own campaign, or — with no character loaded — your active campaign selection, so a GM/admin running the table (not playing a specific PC) still sees it.
Dice rolled from a character sheet in that campaign post to the log automatically.
Anonymous visitors on a group's public share link see the same log (and Now Showing panel) with no account needed.

topics.title: Saving & Loading Maps
topics.summary: Maps are saved records like everything else in the suite — pick one from the Map dropdown, or start a New one, and Save/Delete gate the same way other tools do.
details: Save only lights up once you've actually changed something since loading — not on a fresh page load, and not right after saving.
Delete is only enabled for maps you own (or have edit-level sharing on) — someone else's shared or public map stays view-only.
Anonymous (signed-out) saves stay local to your own browser, same as every other generator tool in the suite.

topics.title: Entity-Referencing Markers
topics.summary: A marker layer holds real pins, each optionally linked to any other saved record — a Location, NPC, Monster, and so on.
details: Select a marker layer, then click empty space on the map to drop a new pin, or click an existing pin to select and edit it.
A selected pin can be dragged directly on the map to reposition it, and its inspector lets you pick what kind of entity it references and which specific one.
On a real-world (tile) base map, pins are anchored to actual coordinates, so they stay in the right place as you pan and zoom — unlike a flat pixel position, which would drift out of place on zoom.

topics.title: Tiered Views
topics.summary: A View is a named visibility preset that hides some layers from lower-tier viewers — useful for keeping a GM-only secrets layer off a shared or public map.
details: The map's own owner (or anyone with edit-level sharing) always sees every layer, unfiltered — Views only ever apply to someone else viewing a shared or public map.
Each View lists which layers/groups it reveals and which account tiers can see it; leaving a View's tier list empty means it applies to every viewer tier.
If a map has no Views defined at all, every viewer sees every layer — Views are opt-in, not a default restriction.

topics.title: Fixing Specific Attributes
topics.summary: Pick a Creature Type, Archetype, or Role to use that exact value instead of rolling it — leave any of them on "Random" to roll as usual.
details: Each select defaults to "Random". Choosing a value there locks that one axis for the next Generate Monster click — everything you didn't pick still resolves randomly.
Combat Scaling, Signature Feature, and Locked Features work the same way — pin any of them to steer generation without hand-building the whole thing.
These only affect the initial Generate Monster roll — there's no per-attribute reroll on an already-generated monster the way Forge has; regenerate to try a new combination.

topics.title: Combat Scaling
topics.summary: Pick which HP/AC/damage band this monster is generated at — Crucible's rough equivalent of a challenge tier — or leave it on "Random".
details: Each Combat Scaling level defines a base HP, AC, damage-per-round, attack bonus, save DC, and target Feature budget — pinning a level fixes all of those together, not just one stat.
A Role's own mechanical tendencies (HP/AC bands, damage profile) multiply on top of whichever level is used, so two monsters at the same Combat Scaling can still come out noticeably different.
These levels are authored in Loom, not hardcoded — a System can define its own scale.

topics.title: Combat scaling field
topics.summary: Which of this System's Array properties Crucible reads as its Combat Scaling levels.
details: This is a personal preference for this browser, not something saved into the System itself — setting it here won't affect anyone else, or show up when editing the System in Loom.
Defaults to a property literally named "combatScaling" if one exists and nothing is picked here, so existing Systems keep working without needing to set anything.
A different System might use that property for something else, or have no combat-scaling concept at all — picking None here just means Crucible generates without a scaling axis.

topics.title: Creature type field
topics.summary: Which of this System's Array properties Crucible reads as its Creature Type vocabulary.
details: This is a personal preference for this browser, not something saved into the System itself — setting it here won't affect anyone else, or show up when editing the System in Loom.
Defaults to a property literally named "creatureTypes" if one exists and nothing is picked here, so existing Systems keep working without needing to set anything.

Different Systems use different names for this concept (5e's own Creature Type vocabulary vs. another game's "Kind"/"Origin"/whatever it calls its own version) — picking None here just means Crucible generates with no creature-type axis.

topics.title: Locked Features
topics.summary: Pin one or more Features to guarantee they're included, instead of leaving traversal to pick everything on its own.
details: Locked Features are added before traversal runs and count against the budget immediately, the same as the Signature Feature — traversal then fills the remaining required/optional slots around them.
Nothing stops you from locking features that don't share a recipe slot or synergy with each other — traversal still tries to build a coherent result around whatever you've pinned.
Leave this empty to let Crucible pick every feature itself, guided only by the Archetype's recipe and whatever Role/Creature Type you've set.

topics.title: Identity
topics.summary: The resolved Creature Type, Archetype, and Role for this monster, plus its Name — edit the Name directly; the rest comes from generation.
details: Creature Type, Archetype, and Role are each either what you pinned in the overrides above, or a random eligible value if you left it blank — Identity shows whichever it ended up as.
The Name field is the only thing here you edit directly; regenerate the monster to get a new resolved Identity instead.

topics.title: Features
topics.summary: The atomic building blocks selected for this monster — its Signature Feature plus everything traversal pulled in to fill the Archetype's recipe.
details: Every feature shown here was chosen for synergy with what's already selected and for not conflicting with it — traversal never adds a feature that fights with one already picked.
This list is exactly what's saved with the monster — there's no separate hidden layer of mechanics behind it.

topics.title: Multiattack — Attacks
topics.summary: List which of this monster's own Features it attacks with and how many times — the description above computes itself from this list and stays in sync if you rename or edit one of those Features.
details: Add options for a genuine choice ("two Claws, two Bites, or one of each") — use "Add option" to add an alternative combination; each option gets its own row list. A single option shows no extra chrome, since that's the common case.
If a Multiattack's phrasing is too irregular to represent this way, leave it as one empty option — the original imported text is shown exactly as typed instead.
Multiattack itself is one shared Feature across every monster (like Bite or Claw) — this list is this monster's own data, not shared, and saves when you save the monster.

topics.title: Feature — Basic Info
topics.summary: ID, Name, Description, and Budget Cost for the selected Feature.
details: Editable here only for a Feature marked Unique (Loom's own Scope field) — those belong to this one monster alone, so changing them can't affect anything else.
A shared Feature (Bite, Claw, Amphibious, and most everything else) is used by many monsters at once, so these fields stay read-only here — use Edit Feature to open it in Loom instead.

topics.title: Recipe Fulfillment
topics.summary: Shows which of the Archetype's recipe slots (signature, required, optional) got filled, and by which Feature — including any slot traversal couldn't fill.
details: An Archetype's recipe is a signature slot plus required and optional slots, each expecting a Feature tagged for that slot and compatible with the resolved Role/Creature Type.
An unfulfilled optional slot isn't an error — it just means nothing compatible and synergistic was available, and the result is still a usable, honestly-labeled monster.

topics.title: Stats
topics.summary: Armor Class, HP, ability scores, and Initiative Bonus derived from the resolved Combat Scaling level and Role — editable directly if you want to hand-tune the numbers.
details: HP and AC come from the Combat Scaling level's base values, adjusted by the Role's own HP/AC band multipliers — a Brute and a Skirmisher at the same Combat Scaling won't have identical stats.
Ability scores favor whichever ability the Role's damage profile relies on (Strength for melee-leaning roles, Dexterity for ranged-leaning ones), with Constitution scaled to the HP band.
Initiative Bonus is the standard ability-modifier math on Dexterity — it's what the Combat Tracker's "Roll Initiative" button uses for this monster once it's added to an encounter.

topics.title: Notes (optional)
topics.summary: Optional. Type your own note directly, or use Generate Note to have Claude write one from this monster's resolved Creature Type, Archetype, Role, and Features.
details: A monster is complete without a note — every generated value already stands on its own as the record.
Generate Note sends the resolved axes and selected Features to Claude and fills this box with its response; whatever's in the box when you Save is what gets saved.

topics.title: Relationships
topics.summary: Tie this Monster to any other record — an NPC, a Location, another Monster, a Character — with a label you type yourself: "Prey of," "Pack with," "Serves," anything.
details: Pick a target kind, choose the specific record, then type a relationship (a small suggestion list appears, but any text works).
Relationships show up on BOTH ends automatically — link a monster as "Pack with" another, and the other's own list shows the same tie right back.
List shows every relationship as text; Graph (the icon next to the section title) shows the same data as a visual web, centered on this Monster.
Open jumps straight to the other record's own tool (Forge/Sanctum/Crucible/Workbench, whichever owns that kind).

topics.title: Locked Features
topics.summary: Pin one or more Features to guarantee they're included in generation, instead of leaving traversal to pick everything on its own.
details: Locked Features are added before traversal runs and spend from (or, if negative, refund into) the budget immediately, the same as the Signature Effect.
