Traversal then repeatedly adds whichever remaining feature has the strongest synergy with what's locked/selected so far and still fits the remaining budget — a zero-synergy feature is never pulled in automatically.
Leave this empty to let Vault pick everything itself, guided only by the resolved Properties and Signature Effect.

topics.title: Budget ceiling field
topics.summary: Which one Property Vault treats as the generator economy's ceiling-setter, for the currently selected System.
details: Picks exactly one of this System's generator-property fields (e.g. Rarity) whose chosen value's Target budget becomes the overall budget ceiling for generation — every other Property with Cost values spends from that ceiling.

This is a personal preference for this browser — setting it here won't affect anyone else, or show up when editing the System in Loom. A different System can have a completely different field (or none) picked here with zero effect on any other System.

A Property can carry Target budget values without being the ceiling-setter (e.g. Combat Scaling tracks its own per-CR budget, unrelated to this economy) — this setting is what tells Vault which one actually counts.
Leave at None to fall back to Vault's built-in default target budget with no field-driven ceiling.

topics.title: Identity
topics.summary: The resolved Properties (Rarity, Activation, Item Form, etc.) for this effect, plus its Name — edit the Name directly; the rest comes from generation.
details: Each Property is either what you pinned in the overrides above, or a random eligible value if you left it blank.
Whichever Property is picked as the Budget ceiling field (see that topic) sets the Feature budget's target ceiling; every other Property's chosen value spends from (or refunds into) that budget.
The Name field is the only thing here you edit directly; regenerate the effect to get a new resolved set of Properties instead.

topics.title: Features
topics.summary: The Signature Effect plus every Feature traversal pulled in to build toward the budget — add or remove Features here to hand-build or tweak the result.
details: Add a Feature from the select below the list at any time; going over budget is allowed and shown as a warning in the Remaining figure rather than blocked outright.

Every Feature shown was chosen for synergy with what's already selected and for not conflicting with it during generation — hand-adding one doesn't run that same check, so a manual add can introduce a conflict traversal would have avoided.
Target/Spent/Remaining recompute live on every add or remove, using the same budget math the automatic generator itself uses.

topics.title: Feature — Basic Info
topics.summary: ID, Name, Description, and Budget Cost for the selected Feature.
details: Always read-only here — every Vault Feature is shared across many spells/items by design, so changing one from a single Effect's own inspector would silently change it everywhere else it's used too.
Use Edit Feature to open it in Loom instead, if it genuinely needs changing.

topics.title: Notes (optional)
topics.summary: Optional. Type your own note directly, or use Generate Note to have Claude write one from this effect's resolved Properties and Features.
details: An effect is complete without a note — every generated value already stands on its own as the record.
Generate Note sends the resolved Properties and selected Features to Claude and fills this box with its response; whatever's in the box when you Save is what gets saved.

topics.title: Relationships
topics.summary: Tie this Effect to any other record — an NPC, a Monster, a Location, a Character, or another Effect — with a label you type yourself: "Requires," "Counters," "Variant of," anything.
details: Pick a target kind, choose the specific record, then type a relationship (a small suggestion list appears — including "Requires," "Counters," "Variant of," "Crafted from," and "Found in" — but any text works).
Relationships show up on BOTH ends automatically — link an effect as a "Variant of" another, and the other's own list shows the same tie right back.
List shows every relationship as text; Graph (the View toggle above) shows the same data as a visual web, centered on this Effect.
Open jumps straight to the other record's own tool (Forge/Sanctum/Crucible/Workbench, whichever owns that kind).

topics.title: Locked Features
topics.summary: Pin one or more Features to guarantee they're included, instead of leaving traversal to pick everything on its own.
details: Locked Features seed the traversal alongside (or instead of) the automatic random seed feature — traversal then repeatedly adds whichever remaining compatible feature has the strongest synergy with what's already selected.
A zero-synergy feature is never pulled in automatically, the same restraint Crucible/Vault's own traversal applies — locking is the way to force one in regardless.
Leave this empty to let Sanctum pick every feature itself, guided only by the resolved Type/Purpose/Environment.

topics.title: Identity
topics.summary: The resolved Type, Purpose, and Environment for this Location, plus its Name — edit the Name directly; the rest comes from generation or the overrides above.
details: Type and Purpose are each either what you pinned in the overrides above, or a random eligible value if you left it blank; Environment comes from the active System's own environment list, if it defines one.
The Name field is the only thing here you edit directly; regenerate the Location to get a new resolved Type/Purpose/Environment instead.

topics.title: Features
topics.summary: The atomic characteristics selected for this Location — a Fortified Walls, Black Market, or Haunted, for example — chosen for tag compatibility and synergy.
details: Unlike Crucible/Vault, there's no recipe or budget here — one random compatible feature seeds the result, then the best-synergy, non-conflicting candidate is added repeatedly until a randomized target count is reached.
A narrow, specific function ("this place is a shop") is modeled as a Feature, not a Type or Purpose — Type/Purpose stay broad, Features layer on the specifics.
This list is exactly what's saved with the Location — there's no separate hidden layer of mechanics behind it.

topics.title: Assets & Needs
topics.summary: What this Location has (Assets) and lacks (Needs) — usually Resources, but any kind of saved record (an NPC, a Monster) can be linked too.
details: The automatic generator only ever populates these with Resources (1-3 for Assets, then 1-3 more for Needs, excluding whatever Assets already took) — linking a specific NPC/Monster/Effect instead is a manual step, done with the kind + entity pickers below each list.

Assets and Needs share one row shape (kind, linked entity, label, description) and one add-row pattern, the same as Features — they're meant to feel like the same kind of list, not three different UIs.
This is deliberately not a full economy or ledger — Assets/Needs describe what a place has or lacks in broad strokes for a GM to use at the table, not a simulated inventory.

topics.title: Relationships
topics.summary: Tie this Location to any other record — an NPC, a Monster, a Character, or another Location — with a label you type yourself: "Parent of," "Connected to," "Owned by," anything.
details: Pick a target kind, choose the specific record, then type a relationship (a small suggestion list appears — including "Parent of" for containment and "Connected to" for a peer link like a road or tunnel — but any text works).

Relationships show up on BOTH ends automatically. A settlement's own region shows "Parent of → the settlement"; the settlement itself shows "← Parent of" back. "Children" work the same way — every Location another Location points at with "Parent of" just shows up in that child's own list, no separate concept needed.
List shows every relationship as text; Graph (the View toggle above) shows the same data as a visual web, centered on this Location.
Open jumps straight to the other record's own tool (Forge/Sanctum/Crucible/Workbench, whichever owns that kind).

topics.title: Notes (optional)
topics.summary: Optional. Type your own note directly, or use Generate Note to have Claude write one from this Location's resolved Identity and Features.
details: A Location is complete without a note — every generated value already stands on its own as the record.
Generate Note sends the resolved Identity and selected Features to Claude and fills this box with its response; whatever's in the box when you Save is what gets saved.

topics.title: Location Details
topics.summary: Read-only here — Locations, and their Setting/System, are authored in Sanctum. This panel just shows the currently selected Location's basics.
details: Selecting a Location here only picks which one to generate NPCs from — to create a new Location, edit an existing one's Type/Purpose/Environment/Features, or manage its Setting, open Sanctum instead.
Species Weights, Mixing Coefficient, and Setting-Specific Archetypes below are the one part of a Location Forge itself still edits, since they're specifically about how Forge generates NPCs here.

topics.title: Node Palette
topics.summary: Select a node in the tree, then click a palette entry to add it as a child (object fields) or step (pipelines).
details: The palette always adds to whatever's currently selected in the tree — select an Object or With node before clicking a palette entry to add a child field to it, or a Pipeline node to add a step to it.
Field/Custom/Pipeline entries add a new node under an Object; Map/Filter/Flatten/Group By/Sort entries (shown once a Pipeline node is selected) add a new step to it instead.

topics.title: Editing Multiple Grid Cells
topics.summary: With more than one grid cell selected, the Custom Properties editor applies whatever you set to every selected cell at once.
details: There's no per-cell distinction shown while multiple cells are selected — every property edit here is applied identically across the whole selection.
Select a single cell instead if you need to see or edit that one cell's own values without affecting its neighbors.

topics.title: Adding Grid Cells to a Group
topics.summary: Selecting a Group makes its map cells directly clickable — click a cell to add it, or click-and-drag to sweep several in at once.
details: Click or drag directly on the grid while this group is selected — every cell you click or sweep over is added to this group immediately, no separate Add step. This only ever adds cells, never removes them — to remove one, use its own Remove button in the Members list below.
If the map has more than one grid layer and this group has no Fog of War link to one, a "Paint on layer" field appears here to pick which layer your clicks target.

The older select-then-add flow still works too: select grid cells on the map while a Layer (not a Group) is selected, then come back here and click Add selected cells — useful if you want to build up a selection before deciding which group it belongs to.

topics.title: Fog of War
topics.summary: Fog of War hides every cell on this grid layer from non-owner viewers except whichever ones are in its Reveal Group — turning it on creates that Group empty, which is why nothing changes until you add cells to it.
details: Add cells the same way as any Group: select grid cells on the map, then select the auto-created Group (named "<Layer name> — Revealed") in the left pane's Groups list and click Add selected cells.

You won't see the fog while editing here — the map's own owner always sees every cell unfiltered, same rule Views follow. Check it from the Dashboard's Map widget as a player, or a shared/public link, to see what a real viewer sees.
A Reveal Group with no members yet is exactly what "Fog of War on, nothing revealed" looks like — not a bug.

topics.title: Walls & Doors
topics.summary: Click each vertex to draw a wall; double-click or Enter to finish. A wall blocks both token movement and fog-of-war vision.
details: Click adds a vertex, with a dashed line previewing the next segment. Double-click or Enter finishes the wall; Escape cancels the whole thing; Backspace removes just the last vertex placed.
Switch to Door in the type picker before drawing to place a door instead — a door always commits as soon as its 2nd point is placed, no double-click needed.
A wall's shape is set entirely by the placement gesture — there's no post-placement vertex editing, only Delete and redraw.

topics.title: Secret & Locked Doors
topics.summary: Secret makes a door render exactly like a plain wall to non-GM viewers; Locked lets players see it's a door but not open it.
details: Secret and Locked are independent — a door can be either, both, or neither.

You (the GM) always retain full control via the inspector's Open/Close Door button regardless of either flag — Secret/Locked only ever restrict what a player can do by clicking the door themselves on the Dashboard's Map widget.
A secret door looks identical to a plain wall for anyone without full map access, with no click response at all — only your own view shows a small tick marking it as a door.

topics.title: Dynamic Lights
topics.summary: A placed light both glows AND unveils fog-of-war within its own radius, wall-aware — like a torch, not just a cosmetic effect.
details: Range, Color, and Opacity are all editable after placement in the inspector.
A light's glow never shines through a wall — it's clipped to the same wall-aware visibility it uses to reveal fog, independent of whether Fog of War is even turned on for the grid layer.
Attach a light to a token (its own inspector field) to have it move with that marker — a torch a character is carrying — instead of staying at a fixed point on the map.

topics.title: Auto-Reveal from Character Vision
topics.summary: Automatically unveils fog-of-war around any character-linked marker with a nonzero Vision Range, wall-aware, as it moves.
details: Only affects markers that both reference a Character and have a Vision Range set directly on the marker itself (in that marker's own inspector) — it's never inherited from the Character record automatically.
Vision Range can be a plain number, or Bound/a Formula against a field on that marker's own linked Character (e.g. a numeric Darkvision-equivalent stat, if that Character's System defines one).
Works alongside manually-painted reveal cells and any placed Lights — all three sources union together into what's currently visible.

topics.title: Tags, Groups, & Display Pills
topics.summary: Tags are plain freeform text, but two prefixes are meaningful to the page list on the left: group: and display:.
details: A tag like group:Location puts this page under a "Location" group in the list on the left — group: names can contain a / to nest, e.g. group:Sessions/Arc 1.
A tag like display:Important shows "Important" as a small pill next to this page's title in the list — a page can have more than one display: tag.
There's no separate place to configure this — the tag's own text is the whole instruction. Any other tag (prefixed or not) is just a normal freeform tag, filterable but otherwise inert.

topics.title: Task Completion Dates
topics.summary: Controls whether checking off a task in View mode adds today's date to the end of the line.
details: On (default): checking a task adds a date, like ✅ 2026-07-27, to the end of the line.
Off: checking a task just marks it done — nothing is added to the line.
Unchecking a task always removes its date, regardless of this setting.

topics.title: Search Scope
topics.summary: Controls whether the page search box also searches inside page contents, not just titles and tags.
details: On (default): the search box matches against a page's title, tags, AND its full body text — so it finds a page by anything written inside it, not just its name.
Off: only titles and tags are searched — narrower, useful once a wiki has enough pages that a common word turns up matches in dozens of unrelated bodies.
A page that only matches in its body (not its title) still shows up in the list — the group tree auto-expands to reveal it while a search is active.

topics.title: Parent Pages
topics.summary: Set another page as this one's parent to nest it underneath that page in the list on the left.
details: A page can have one parent. Setting one nests this page under it in the list on the left, however many levels deep.
This is different from a tag-based group or a Related link — it's a real parent/child relationship between two specific pages, not just a shared label or a loose reference.

topics.title: Quests
topics.summary: A [!quest] callout, with an ordinary markdown checklist inside it, IS a quest — no separate quest editor or record.
details: Write > [!quest] Quest Name, then a normal markdown checklist underneath for objectives — status (Not Started/Active/Complete) is shown automatically, worked out from how many boxes are checked, not something you set yourself.
Reference an NPC, location, monster, or anything else right inside an objective the same way you would anywhere else on the page: `npc:Name`, `location:Name`, and so on.

[[Quest Name]] links to a quest the same way [[Page Title]] links to a page — page titles are checked first, so a quest link only ever kicks in when no page has that exact title. [[Page Title#Quest Name]] is always unambiguous, even if two different pages each have a quest with the same name.
A quest is scoped to the page it's written on — its title only needs to be unique on that one page.

topics.title: Story Boards
topics.summary: A [!story-board] callout, with a couple of metadata lines plus a Nodes table and an Edges table, IS an interactive planning board — no separate Library kind.
details: Write > [!story-board] Board Name, then Layout: freeform or swimlane, and (for swimlane) Lanes: and Stages: as comma-separated lists.

The Nodes table lists each card: its own Node name (also its reference key for the Edges table), an optional Type (ref/placeholder), an optional Ref (a kindId:Name or quest:Title compound reference, same syntax as an inline reference chip), and freeform Lane/Stage/X/Y/Color.
The Edges table connects nodes by name: From, To, and an optional Label.
A board is scoped to the page it's written on, and multiple boards are allowed per page — same 'unique per page' convention Quests use.
Switch between Freeform (drag cards anywhere) and Swimlane (lane × stage grid) at any time from the canvas toolbar — both layouts are stored on the same node, so switching never loses data.

topics.title: Relationships
topics.summary: A read-only diagram of how your existing pages, quests, and referenced Library content connect to each other — built automatically from what's already written, not something you author separately.
details: Every [[Page Title]] wikilink draws a page-to-page connection; a link that matches a quest's own title instead connects to that quest.
Every inline reference (npc:, location:, monster:, and so on) anywhere on a page draws a connection from that page to the referenced record.

Computed when you open the view (or after a page save), not kept live — it deliberately does NOT ingest a Story Board's own internal planning layout, since that's a separate GM-only planning surface, not existing campaign content.

topics.title: Timeline
topics.summary: A day-sorted list of every `date:` reference across the whole workspace, grouped by day — built automatically from what's already written, same as Relationships.
details: Every `date:<day>` (or `date:current`/`date:today`) reference on any page shows up here, grouped under its own day heading and formatted using the active Setting's own calendar.
A "Today" divider splits past entries from upcoming ones, using the same live ambient date the Calendar widget itself reads/writes.
Click any entry to jump straight to the page it came from.
Computed when you open the tab (or after a page save), not kept live — same "computed on demand" principle Relationships uses.

topics.title: Date References
topics.summary: A `date:<day>` inline code span renders as a formatted date chip against your campaign's active calendar — a deadline, a discovered-on date, or a due date attached to a quest or objective.
details: `date:123` shows Day 123 formatted using the active Setting's own calendar (or a plain "Day 123" if that Setting has none). Negative numbers count backward from the campaign's own Day 0 start.
`date:current` (or `date:today`) always shows the campaign's own live ambient date, wherever it's read, rather than a fixed day baked into the page.
Add a custom label with a pipe: `date:30|Festival begins` shows "Festival begins: <formatted date>".
Purely informational — a date chip has no click action; it doesn't yet drive overdue tracking or a timeline view.
